problems.title: Thermal efficiency of an engine
problems.scenario:
A heat engine receives **1000 kJ** of heat and produces **400 kJ** of net work.

Find its **thermal efficiency** (as a decimal fraction).
hints: Just divide the work by the heat input.
problems.solution:
Thermal efficiency is the fraction of heat input turned into work:

$$\eta_{th} = \frac{W_{net}}{Q_H} = \frac{400}{1000} = 0.40$$

So 40% becomes work and the other 600 kJ is rejected to the sink.

problems.title: Work from efficiency
problems.scenario:
A power plant has a thermal efficiency of **0.35** and receives **500 kJ** of heat.

Find the **net work** produced, in kJ.
problems.solution:
Rearrange the efficiency definition for work:

$$W_{net} = \eta_{th}\,Q_H = 0.35 \times 500 = 175\ \text{kJ}$$

The remaining $Q_L = Q_H - W_{net} = 325\ \text{kJ}$ is rejected.

problems.title: Carnot efficiency
problems.scenario:
A reversible heat engine operates between a source at **800 K** and a sink at **300 K**.

Find its **(Carnot) thermal efficiency**, as a decimal fraction.
hints: Temperatures must be absolute (they're in K).
problems.solution:
The maximum possible efficiency between two reservoirs is the Carnot value:

$$\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{300}{800} = 1 - 0.375 = 0.625$$

No real engine between these two temperatures can beat 62.5%.

problems.title: Refrigerator COP
problems.scenario:
A refrigerator removes **400 kJ** of heat from the cold space using **100 kJ** of work input.

Find its **coefficient of performance** $COP_R$.
hints: For a fridge, the desired output is the heat removed $Q_L$.
problems.solution:
A refrigerator's performance is the cooling delivered per unit of work:

$$COP_R = \frac{Q_L}{W_{net,in}} = \frac{400}{100} = 4$$

A COP above 1 is normal — you're *moving* heat, not creating it, so you get more cooling than the work you put in.

problems.title: Heat pump work input
problems.scenario:
A heat pump delivers **8.0 kW** of heating to a house and has a coefficient of performance $COP_{HP} = 2.5$.

Find the **electric power input**, in kW.
hints: For a heat pump the desired output is the heat delivered $\dot Q_H$.
$COP_{HP} = \dot Q_H/\dot W$, so rearrange for $\dot W$.
problems.solution:
Rearrange the heat-pump COP for the work input:

$$COP_{HP} = \frac{\dot Q_H}{\dot W} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dot W = \frac{\dot Q_H}{COP_{HP}} = \frac{8.0}{2.5} = 3.2\ \text{kW}$$

The other $8.0 - 3.2 = 4.8\ \text{kW}$ is heat drawn from the cold outdoor air — which is why a heat pump beats a resistance heater.

problems.title: Carnot refrigerator power
problems.scenario:
A reversible (Carnot) refrigerator keeps a cold room at **−8 °C** while rejecting heat to surroundings at **25 °C**. It removes heat at **5.0 kW**.

Find the **minimum power input**, in kW.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — kelvin:** $T_L = -8 + 273 = 265\ \text{K}$, $T_H = 25 + 273 = 298\ \text{K}$.

**Step 2 — best possible COP** (reversible):

$$COP_{R,rev} = \frac{T_L}{T_H - T_L} = \frac{265}{298 - 265} = \frac{265}{33} = 8.03$$

**Step 3 — minimum power** for 5.0 kW of cooling:

$$\dot W = \frac{\dot Q_L}{COP_{R,rev}} = \frac{5.0}{8.03} = 0.623\ \text{kW}$$

Any real fridge between these temperatures needs *more* than 0.62 kW.

problems.title: Maximum work from a heat source
problems.scenario:
A heat engine takes **2000 kJ** of heat from a source at **900 K** and rejects heat to a sink at **300 K**.

Find the **maximum possible work** output, in kJ.
hints: Maximum work comes from a reversible (Carnot) engine.
problems.solution:
The most work you can extract corresponds to the Carnot efficiency:

$$\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{300}{900} = 0.6667$$

$$W_{max} = \eta_{th,rev}\,Q_H = 0.6667 \times 2000 = 1333\ \text{kJ}$$

The unavoidable $2000 - 1333 = 667\ \text{kJ}$ must be rejected to the sink — the second law forbids doing better.

problems.title: Carnot heat pump for a house
problems.scenario:
A house is kept at **22 °C** while the outside air is at **−5 °C**. The house loses heat at **60 000 kJ/h**. A reversible (Carnot) heat pump supplies the heating.

Find the **minimum power input**, in kW.
hints: Convert temperatures to kelvin and the heat loss to kW: $60\,000\ \text{kJ/h} \div 3600 = 16.67\ \text{kW}$.
Carnot heat-pump COP: $COP_{HP,rev} = T_H/(T_H - T_L)$, with $T_H = 295$, $T_L = 268\ \text{K}$.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — convert units:** $T_H = 295\ \text{K}$, $T_L = 268\ \text{K}$; heat demand $\dot Q_H = 60\,000/3600 = 16.67\ \text{kW}$ (the steady loss must be replaced).

**Step 2 — best COP:**

$$COP_{HP,rev} = \frac{T_H}{T_H - T_L} = \frac{295}{295 - 268} = \frac{295}{27} = 10.93$$

**Step 3 — minimum power:**

$$\dot W = \frac{\dot Q_H}{COP_{HP,rev}} = \frac{16.67}{10.93} = 1.525\ \text{kW}$$

A small temperature gap gives a huge COP — only ~1.5 kW of electricity replaces 16.7 kW of heat loss.
